overview.summary: Professional athletes compete in sport as their job, training and performing at a high level for clubs, teams or as individuals. Very few people who play sport when young become full-time professionals.
overview.problems: They entertain and inspire spectators, and train to push physical and mental limits.
overview.worksWith: Coaches, teammates, physiotherapists, doctors, nutritionists, sports psychologists, agents and managers.
overview.workplaces: Training grounds, gyms, stadiums and competition venues, with a lot of travel.

timeline.title: Training session
timeline.description: The athlete practises skills, tactics and fitness work set by the coach.
timeline.why: Elite performance comes from repeated, focused practice.

timeline.title: Strength and conditioning
timeline.description: The athlete does gym work to build strength, speed and resilience to injury.
timeline.why: A stronger body copes better with the demands of the sport.

timeline.title: Recovery and nutrition
timeline.description: The athlete eats planned meals, rests and uses recovery methods such as stretching.
timeline.why: Recovery is when the body adapts to training.

timeline.title: Team meetings and video analysis
timeline.description: The athlete studies performances and plans for the next opponent.
timeline.why: Understanding the game improves decisions during it.

timeline.title: Second session, treatment or media
timeline.description: Some athletes train again, receive physiotherapy or do interviews and sponsor commitments.
timeline.why: Looking after the body and the public side of the job are both part of the work.

timeline.title: Competing
timeline.description: The athlete travels, warms up and performs under pressure.
timeline.why: Everything else in the week prepares for this.

responsibilities: Training regularly and following the coach's plan
Looking after your body through sleep, nutrition and recovery
Working with coaches and medical staff
challenges: Very few people reach professional level, and many do not make it despite great effort.
Injuries can end a career early.
Careers are often short, so planning for life after sport matters.
There is performance pressure and public criticism.
Frequent travel means time away from family.
Income varies hugely between sports and levels.
Rules about doping, diet and behaviour are strict.
workEnvironment: Training grounds, gyms and competition venues, with frequent travel and a structured routine. Match and training schedules decide your week, including weekends and holidays. Athletes work closely with a support team.
rewards: Doing what you love at a high level
tradeoffs: Pay and opportunities that vary hugely by sport, country and level

activity.title: Keep a four-week skill log for one sport skill
steps: Choose one safe skill in a sport you play, such as free throws, a passing drill or a running distance.
Test your starting level and write it down.
Practise three times a week for about 20 minutes, with a warm-up, and record your results.
After four weeks, compare your first and last numbers and note what helped.
Ask your coach or a teacher what to improve next.
activity.outcome: You practise setting a goal, training regularly and measuring progress.
activity.safety: Warm up and cool down, stop if anything hurts, and talk to a doctor, coach or teacher before any intense training. Do not use supplements or follow extreme diets.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
